questions.problem: Given $X∼\text{Geom}(\frac{3}{4}),$ compute $P(X=3).$
questions.worked_solution:
If $X∼\text{Geom}(p),$ then $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}(1-p)^{x-1}p, & x=1,2,3,… \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Here, $X∼\text{Geom}(\frac{3}{4}),$ so the distribution of $X$ in this case is

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}{(\frac{1}{4})}^{x-1}(\frac{3}{4}), & x=1,2,3,… \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=3) & =f(3) \\  & ={(\frac{1}{4})}^{2}(\frac{3}{4}) \\  & =\frac{3}{64}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given $X∼\text{Geom}(0.4),$ compute $P(X\ge 4)$ rounded to $3$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
If $X∼\text{Geom}(p),$ then $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}(1-p)^{x-1}p, & x=1,2,3,… \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Here, $X∼\text{Geom}(0.4),$ so the distribution of $X$ in this case is

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}{(0.6)}^{x-1}(0.4), & x=1,2,3… \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

There are infinitely many values of $X$ such that $X\ge 4.$ However, we can simplify the computation by using the complement instead:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 4) & =1-P(X<4)\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the complement, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<4) & =P(X\in {1,2,3}) \\  & =P(X=1)+P(X=2)+P(X=3) \\  & =f(1)+f(2)+f(3) \\  & ={(0.6)}^{0}(0.4)+{(0.6)}^{1}(0.4)+{(0.6)}^{2}(0.4) \\  & =0.784.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 4) & =1-P(X<4) \\  & =1-0.784 \\  & =0.216.\end{aligned}
$$

If $X \sim \textrm{Geom}(p),$ then $X$ has the following probability mass function:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14069741/assets/e31c12bf515605c7cb46d96a55a8e2a3cab7eaeb5897bb04cfbe87d4d6cc6875.png)

Here, $X \sim \textrm{Geom}\left(\dfrac 37\right),$ so the distribution of $X$ in this case is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14069741/assets/5e7f6f2abab85141723e1ef5bd97157968584623433cd5a3e4d0454a39ef000b.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<5) & =P(X\in {1,2,3,4}) \\  & =P(X=1)+P(X=2)+P(X=3)+P(X=4) \\  & =f(1)+f(2)+f(3)+f(4) \\  & ={(\frac{4}{7})}^{0}(\frac{3}{7})+{(\frac{4}{7})}^{1}(\frac{3}{7})+{(\frac{4}{7})}^{2}(\frac{3}{7})+{(\frac{4}{7})}^{3}(\frac{3}{7}) \\  & ≈0.893\end{aligned}
$$

to  $3$ decimal places.

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Computing a Probability Over a Bounded Interval: Lower Bound is Not Zero
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If $X \sim \textrm{Geom}(p),$ then $X$ has the following probability mass function:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14069741/assets/e31c12bf515605c7cb46d96a55a8e2a3cab7eaeb5897bb04cfbe87d4d6cc6875.png)

Here, $X \sim \textrm{Geom}\left(\dfrac 15\right),$ so the distribution of $X$ in this case is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14069741/assets/cb4d54529b778e27c44ea6611a366eef6e540d9de5343e3425797f03d51c54de.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(2\le X\le 3) & =P(X\in {2,3}) \\  & =P(X=2)+P(X=3) \\  & =f(2)+f(3) \\  & ={(\frac{4}{5})}^{1}(\frac{1}{5})+{(\frac{4}{5})}^{2}(\frac{1}{5}) \\  & =\frac{36}{125}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Computing a Probability Over a Bounded Interval Using the Complement
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If $X \sim \textrm{Geom}(p),$ then $X$ has the following probability mass function:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14069741/assets/ab3f034397a81b2369008754aef3c05f998f180b5127e543a05ab408c743cf8a.png)

Here, $X \sim \textrm{Geom}\left(\dfrac 56\right),$ so the distribution of $X$ in this case is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14069741/assets/efc7a45d9b19867340454ad32abe129214dcca021394f259f79d1e26643da5c7.png)

There are infinitely many values of $X$ such that $X > 2.$ However, we can simplify the computation by using the complement instead:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X>2) & =1-P(X\le 2)\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the complement, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 2) & =P(X\in {1,2}) \\  & =P(X=1)+P(X=2) \\  & =f(1)+f(2) \\  & ={(\frac{1}{6})}^{0}(\frac{5}{6})+{(\frac{1}{6})}^{1}(\frac{5}{6}) \\  & =\frac{35}{36}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X>2) & =1-P(X\le 2) \\  & =1-\frac{35}{36} \\  & =\frac{1}{36}.\end{aligned}
$$
